The identity D_t² = Σ λ_l^{2t}(ψ_l(x) − ψ_l(y))² is exact. The paper's Proposition 1 says the truncated map keeps it "up to relative accuracy δ". The true bound is absolute and can be large relative to D_t for nearby points. In the refinement sense, the diffusion-map family coarsens with t only through the threshold. Finite sets, counting measure and reversible walks only. It says nothing about the manifold limit or about non-reversible chains. | Active |
| [THEORY-746](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-746.md) | Over a fixed finite set of basis functions, slow feature analysis is a generalized eigenproblem: the outputs that minimize ⟨ẏ²⟩ under zero mean, unit variance and decorrelation are the bottom generalized eigenvectors of the derivative covariance against the covariance, in order of slowness, and a stack of such stages, each of whose function spaces contains its inputs, can only keep or lower each of its first m slowness values on the training signal, and may keep them | Wiskott and Sejnowski (2002), [LIT-1249](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1249.md), read in full in [NOTE-971](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-971.md). Within the span of a fixed basis, the slowest decorrelated unit-variance outputs are the bottom generalized eigenvectors of the pencil (⟨ż̃ż̃ᵀ⟩, cov z̃), and each output's slowness is its eigenvalue. A consequence the paper does not draw: a stack of such stages whose function spaces contain their inputs is never faster at a higher stage, componentwise, on the training signal, so in this model "higher is slower" is imposed by the objective, weakly, and can stall. It is about the training signal and a fixed function space. It says nothing about test data, about a generative model, about invariance as opposed to slowness, or about learning dynamics. | Active |
| [THEORY-759](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-759.md) | A six-layer, 256-unit ReLU network trained by full-batch Adam to regress a sum of sinusoids at 5 to 50 cycles on [0, 1] fits the components in order of frequency, and keeps that order when the amplitudes rise tenfold with frequency, so in this setting the order of acquisition is set by the learner and not by the strength of the target's components | Rahaman et al. (2019), [LIT-1261](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1261.md), Experiment 1, read in full in [NOTE-983](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-983.md). With equal amplitudes, and with amplitudes rising from 0.1 at 5 cycles to 1 at 50, the normalised fit \|f̃(k_i)\|/A_i reaches 1 at low frequency first. This is the reverse of the order by strength that [THEORY-186](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-186.md) gives for a deep linear network. One architecture, one optimiser, a 1-D input, ten runs averaged. The paper's theory gives a bound on speed, not this order. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-775](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-775.md) | With a Gaussian random-walk prior and an instantaneous unit-variance Gaussian encoder, the KL half of the evidence lower bound is the unordered slowness loss plus a constant; with a linear Gaussian encoder and decoder on whitened input, the bound is maximized on the span of the slowest SFA directions whose lag-one autocorrelation exceeds one half, with the basis inside that span unidentified, and on unwhitened input the maximizer is neither SFA's subspace nor invariant to rescaling the input | Schüler and Wiskott (2025), [LIT-1296](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1296.md), read in full in [NOTE-1015](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1015.md). The ELBO of a dynamical VAE with prior N(z_{t−1}, I) and encoder N(g(x_t), I) is Σ E log p(x_t \| z_t) − ½Σ‖g(x_{t−1}) − g(x_t)‖² − (T − 1)d/2, an exact identity. For linear Gaussian encoder and decoder on whitened input, the maximizer spans the bottom eigenvectors of the difference covariance with eigenvalue μ < 1, each scaled by (μ^{−1/2} − 1)^{1/2} and then rotated arbitrarily. So it recovers SFA's slow span, cut at lag-one autocorrelation ½, not SFA's features. On raw input it trades variance against slowness. It says nothing about nonlinear encoders, about predictive sufficiency, or about Turner and Sahani's model. | Active |
| [THEORY-782](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-782.md) | In networks that learn addition from summed embeddings, the critical training fraction of grokking is the fraction at which the training set's same-answer pairs come to fix the generalising representation up to translation and scale, at every group size, as Liu, Kitouni, Nolte, Michaud, Tegmark and Williams propose | Liu, Kitouni, Nolte, Michaud, Tegmark and Williams (2022), [LIT-858](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-858.md), read in [NOTE-662](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-662.md), with Power et al.'s critical fraction ([LIT-341](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-341.md)). The paper presents the critical training fraction as where the training set's equations fix the embedding. [THEORY-181](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-181.md) holds the theorem for the ideal model and the match at the one size measured, p = 10 with 1D embeddings. Held to addition: for S₃ the networks generalise beyond this mechanism. The multi-size test is [QUESTION-199](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-199.md). | Proposed |
| [THEORY-786](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-786.md) | Deep networks learn hierarchically generated data from a number of examples set by when the correlations between input patches and the class rise above sampling noise, so detecting those correlations is how they learn the grammar, as Cagnetta and coauthors propose | Cagnetta, Petrini, Tomasini, Favero and Wyart (2023), [LIT-877](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-877.md), propose that deep networks learn compositional data by detecting the correlations between input patches and the class, and that the sample complexity is where those correlations emerge from sampling noise. The record holds as shown, in [THEORY-195](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-195.md), the measured law and the synonym-invariance it coincides with. This is the mechanism, filed under [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) v4 when the narrowing dropped it. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-788](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-788.md) | Training a deep classifier past zero training error generally collapses its last-layer features onto their class means, drives the centred means toward a simplex equiangular tight frame aligned with the classifier, and makes the decision nearest class mean, as Papyan, Han and Donoho propose from their runs | Papyan, Han and Donoho (2020), [LIT-618](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-618.md), title their paper on the "prevalence" of neural collapse and present it as a pervasive outcome of the terminal phase of training. The record holds as shown, in [THEORY-083](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-083.md), only what their runs measured: three architectures with cross-entropy on seven balanced datasets without augmentation. This is the general law, filed under [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) v4 when the narrowing dropped it. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-789](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-789.md) | The block coarse-graining that maximizes mutual information with the system beyond a buffer picks out the renormalization-group-relevant variables in general, so those variables can be found from samples by information alone, without being known beforehand, as Koch-Janusz and Ringel propose | Koch-Janusz and Ringel (2017), [LIT-873](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-873.md), propose that their mutual-information criterion finds a system's relevant degrees of freedom with no prior knowledge of them. What the record holds as shown, [THEORY-194](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-194.md), is that it recovered variables renormalization already uses, on 2D models whose answer was known. This is the general thesis that result was offered for, filed under [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) v4 when the narrowing dropped it. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-793](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-793.md) | Gradient flow on a symmetrized Barlow Twins loss with a linear or fixed-kernel model, from generic small initialization and not only from initialization aligned with the eigenvectors, learns the top eigenvectors of the pairs' symmetrized cross-correlation one at a time in order of eigenvalue and ends at a top spectral solution, as Simon and coauthors derive informally | Simon et al. (2023), [LIT-242](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-242.md), read in [NOTE-741](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-741.md). The stepwise dynamics, the minimum-norm end point and the kernel-PCA form are proved from aligned initialization, and that part is the Active [THEORY-229](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-229.md). Generic small initialization rests on the paper's Result 4.6, which its authors style a result and derive informally in App. C, with numerical checks at d = 3. This THEORY holds that generic case. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-794](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-794.md) | In vision models, compositional generalization to unseen combinations of concepts is driven by the diversity of the combinations seen in training rather than by data volume, and arrives with representations that are linearly factored by concept, as Uselis, Dittadi and Oh propose | Uselis, Dittadi & Oh (2025), [LIT-667](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-667.md), read in [NOTE-525](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-525.md). Their title and abstract present diversity of combinations, not data volume, as what drives compositional generalization in vision models. Their evidence is ResNet-50s trained from scratch on two-concept grids, with checkpoints chosen on the unseen pairs, and that measured part, with the factorization theorem, is the Active [THEORY-117](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-117.md). This THEORY holds the general causal claim. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-797](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-797.md) | Deep classifiers trained with MSE loss stay near the least-squares classifier for their own features and move along the central path by the dynamics of continually renormalized gradient flow, whose equal-rate growth of the whitened class-separation singular values is how they reach neural collapse, as Han, Papyan and Donoho propose | Han, Papyan & Donoho (2021; ICLR 2022), [LIT-974](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-974.md), read in [NOTE-783](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-783.md). The paper's proposed explanation of neural collapse under MSE in real networks, filed apart from its measured central-path proximity and its derivation in a renormalized model ([THEORY-278](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-278.md)) under [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) v4. Renormalization is imposed, not measured, and every experiment used weight decay, which the derivation excludes. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-798](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-798.md) | Independently trained neural encoders of the same data learn latent spaces that differ mainly by an angle-preserving map, a rotation or reflection times a rescaling, so their cosine similarities to shared anchor samples agree across seeds, architectures and languages, as Moschella et al. propose | Moschella, Maiorca, Fumero, Norelli, Locatello & Rodolà (2022; ICLR 2023), [LIT-849](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-849.md), read in [NOTE-652](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-652.md). The hypothesis behind relative representations, filed apart from what their experiments measured ([THEORY-175](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-175.md)) under [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) v4. The source assumes it and tests it only through its consequences; it never fits a map between two spaces. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-802](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-802.md) v2 | In trained networks as in constructed ones, interchange interventions on a fixed set of variables can be satisfied equally by alignments related by a change of basis, so which internal direction mediates a high-level variable is fixed only relative to a chosen decomposition into units, and complex models will generally have several distinct, fully correct abstractions | The general reading that [THEORY-243](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-243.md) held before the promotion audit narrowed it to the three-unit network it proves (batch 062). Wu et al. (2024), [LIT-961](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-961.md), conjecture that complex models have "multiple distinct fully correct abstractions" and that the causal-abstraction framework cannot settle structural equivalence; Makelov et al. (2023), [LIT-968](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-968.md), §8, grant that crossing component boundaries makes "illusory" tenuous, and answer by privileging components. Filed under [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) v4 so the wide form stays a thesis evidence can confirm or reject. Its only support is the constructed tie. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-805](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-805.md) | Volume-maximizing joint-embedding objectives as a class, VICReg and SimCLR as well as MSN and SwAV, carry a prior toward equal-sized clusters, and that prior costs them semantic transfer when the pretraining data are class-imbalanced, including on naturally long-tailed data | The general reading that [THEORY-306](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-306.md) held before the promotion audit narrowed it to the explicit priors of MSN and SwAV and to one experiment with two to eight classes per batch (batch 033). Assran et al. (2022), [LIT-231](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-231.md), read in [NOTE-850](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-850.md), argue the prior for the whole class, VICReg through an informal reduction to K-means and SimCLR through a cited equivalence, and read it as the cause of the degradation reported on real long-tailed data. Filed under [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) v4 so the wide form stays a thesis evidence can confirm or reject. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-808](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-808.md) | Transformers trained by next-token prediction on sequence processes whose latent dynamics factor as a tensor product learn to represent the belief state in approximately orthogonal per-factor subspaces of about the factored dimension rather than the joint one, and reach that factored representation first even when noise makes it lossy | The general reading that [THEORY-256](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-256.md) held before the promotion audit narrowed it to the five Mess3 and Bloch Walk factors and the 4-layer GPT-2-style models tested (batch 019). Shai et al. (2026), [LIT-986](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-986.md), read in [NOTE-758](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-758.md), present next-token training (the paper is titled “Transformers learn factored representations”) as yielding factored, orthogonal belief representations; [NOTE-758](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-758.md)'s claims C2 to C4 are each shown on one family of synthetic processes. Filed under [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) v4 so the wide form stays a thesis evidence can confirm or reject. It does not include the paper's inference that the preference is architectural (C5), which App. D.4 leaves open, or the claim that the factored form persists at convergence under strong noise, which Fig. 12 contradicts. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-813](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-813.md) | Training a wide network in the lazy, kernel regime does not make its features more collapsed than at initialization, so neural collapse, where it occurs, is something only feature learning produces | The general reading that [THEORY-294](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-294.md) held before the promotion audit narrowed it to the one-dimensional, zero-bias, two-class case it proves. Kothapalli and Tirer (2024), [LIT-985](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-985.md), read in [NOTE-774](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-774.md), draw it as their conclusion: the lazy regime does not collapse anything, so the data-dependence of collapse has to come from a kernel that moves with the data. Beyond the solved case their support is simulation on two-class Gaussian data, where the NTK comes out less collapsed than the NNGP. Filed under [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) v4 so the wide form stays a thesis evidence can confirm or reject. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-825](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-825.md) | Hyperbolic graph embedding models trained on task losses that never mention the hierarchy do not place a tree's root nearest the origin, and their distance from the origin orders hierarchical levels only partly | Yang, Zhou, Ying, Chen & King (2023), [LIT-871](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-871.md), read in [NOTE-669](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-669.md), assert for hyperbolic graph models in general what they measured for HGCN on two synthetic trees: the root is not innermost and radius reads level only partly. The general form was the lead clause of [THEORY-421](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-421.md) until that account was narrowed to the measurement on 2026-10-20 ([ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) v4); it is filed here so that it stays a thesis evidence can confirm or reject. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-865](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-865.md) | In Claude language models, a sparse set of residual-stream directions that a corpus-averaged Jacobian lens identifies as verbalizable (the J-space) is causally privileged for verbal report, for holding instructed concepts, for unspoken intermediate steps of reasoning and for passing one argument to many functions, while continuation, anomaly detection and line wrapping use the same information without routing through it; it carries workspace-like content only in a middle band of layers, holds on the order of tens of active directions and under a tenth of activation variance, and is amplified and relayed by the weights more than other directions | Gurnee, Sofroniew et al. (2026), [LIT-1347](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1347.md), read in [NOTE-1069](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1069.md) (main text in full, appendices in part). It is the functional analogue of conscious access, in the access sense only, found in a transformer and tested by intervention. The sharp edge: one company's models studied by that company, a lens whose own statistics draw the layer band, a flexible/automatic split partly defined by the result, and an explicit refusal to say anything about phenomenal consciousness. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-869](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-869.md) | In Claude language models, projecting out the most active J-space directions in early workspace layers lowers the rate of felt, first-person, sensory language in the models' narrations of their own processing and in their descriptions of another person's experience, while norm-matched perturbations along other directions do not and the text stays coherent; so in these models the experiential register of report depends on the access-like workspace and is not specific to self-report | Gurnee, Sofroniew et al. (2026), [LIT-1347](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1347.md), §3.5.3 and §A.23, read in [NOTE-1069](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1069.md). The authors conclude that "the J-space supports the model's propensity to provide rich experiential reports, whether about itself or another entity". The sharp edge: the measure is a register of text graded by another model, on five or six prompts per condition, in one company's models; and the effect holds for reports about others, so it is not evidence of anything the self-reports are about. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-965](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-965.md) | Sparse-autoencoder features of a large language model's residual stream are units the model computes with: they track abstract concepts across languages, modalities and concrete or abstract instances, and intervening on one changes the model's behaviour in the way its label predicts, better than directions found from a few labelled examples | Templeton et al. (2024), [LIT-1533](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1533.md), read in [NOTE-1178](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1178.md), with Bricken et al. (2023), [LIT-1545](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1545.md), for the one-layer case. The thesis of both papers: features are the model's own units, shown by steering. The authors' own hedges: steering needs features clamped beyond their observed range; the reconstruction error rides along; "we haven't rigorously evaluated our features against other steering methods". The record holds a result against it for known causal variables ([THEORY-968](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-968.md)). | Proposed |
| [THEORY-966](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-966.md) | Greedy edge pruning of the ACDC kind, which removes each edge whose removal changes the output metric by less than a threshold given the edges already removed, keeps only one input of a redundant OR gate, and which input it keeps depends on the order in which edges are visited, so when a model has redundant sufficient paths the circuit it returns is one of several sufficient subgraphs | Conmy et al. (2023), [LIT-1547](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1547.md), Appendix M, read in [NOTE-1170](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1170.md). For out = 1 − ReLU(1 − x − y) with x = y = 1, removing either input alone leaves the output at 1, so the first one visited is pruned and the second is then kept; visiting y first keeps x instead. It does not say how common redundant paths are in trained models, nor that any other method does better: HISP keeps neither input. | Active |
| [THEORY-967](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-967.md) | In a two-layer attention-only transformer, attention heads change function during training: heads in the first layer that predict simple n-grams early later become the previous-token heads of the induction circuit, a bracket-matching support head, or supporting members of a circuit with second-layer n-gram heads, giving up simple n-grams as they do, and particular n-grams pass from one head to another; so later circuits form partly by repurposing components that already had a role | Wang, Hoogland, van Wingerden, Furman and Murfet (2024), [LIT-1535](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1535.md), read in [NOTE-1188](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1188.md). "Heads 0:1, 0:4, 0:7 ultimately become the two previous-token heads and (layer 0) Dyck head respectively. However, these heads appear to start out as simple n-gram heads." Layer-0 multigram heads lose information about simple n-grams from stage LM3, as path patching and composition scores show them coming to feed layer-1 bracket-matching heads. The "ago" n-gram moves from head 0:0 to head 1:0. Whether the late roles are built from the early ones, or merely follow them in time, is not tested. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-968](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-968.md) | In the Mechanistic Interpretability Benchmark's causal-variable localization baselines on Gemma-2 2B and Llama-3.1 8B, features of the public Gemma Scope and Llama Scope sparse autoencoders, selected by a learned binary mask, never gave a higher mean interchange-intervention accuracy than the same mask over the model's own hidden dimensions, in all sixteen task–variable cells and by 1 to 14 points, while distributed alignment search, trained against the causal model it is scored on, gave the highest mean in fifteen of them | Mueller et al. (2025), [LIT-1550](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1550.md), read in [NOTE-1169](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1169.md). Unsupervised SAE features were worse units than neurons for known task variables across ARC, MCQA, two-digit addition and RAVEL. It does not say SAE features are never causal units: the comparison is on residual streams, under one selection method, with the base reconstruction error carried into every intervention, and the best method is supervised by the hypothesis it is scored against. | Active |
| [THEORY-970](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-970.md) | On three language-model tasks whose circuits earlier manual work reported, indirect object identification and Greater-Than in GPT-2 Small and Python docstrings in a four-layer attention-only model, ACDC run with resampled corrupted activations against KL divergence ranked the reported edges with areas under the ROC curve of 0.85 to 0.98, above head-importance pruning and subnetwork probing on all three; on two compiled tracr programs it ranked them poorly with corrupted activations, 0.68 and 0.20, and exactly with zero activations | Conmy et al. (2023), [LIT-1547](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1547.md), read in [NOTE-1170](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1170.md). Edge AUCs with corrupted activations and KL: Docstring 0.982, Greater-Than 0.853, IOI 0.869 for ACDC, against 0.805, 0.693, 0.789 for HISP and 0.937, 0.806, 0.823 for SP. It does not say ACDC finds the true circuit: the reported circuits are incomplete, the results depend on metric, ablation and parent order, and negative components are missed at sparse thresholds. | Active |
| [THEORY-971](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-971.md) | A unit that thresholds a pre-activation equal to a term depending only on one operand plus a term depending only on the other cannot be active on exactly the pairs with a given sum when that sum has two decompositions: if it is active on (x, y) and (z, w), it is active on (x, w) or on (z, y); so a sum computed from separately represented operands needs an earlier unit that combines them, as Ameisen et al. argue for addition in language models | Ameisen et al. (2025), [LIT-1552](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1552.md), read in [NOTE-1185](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1185.md), re-derived here. It is why their addition graphs contain "lookup table" features between operand features and sum features. Whether a given unit in a trained model meets the premise is an empirical matter: attention patterns that depend on both operands, or any earlier nonlinearity that mixes them, break it, and that mixing is exactly the intermediate step the result says is required. | Active |
| [THEORY-973](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-973.md) | In small attention-only transformer language models of two to six layers, in-context learning, measured as the loss at token 500 minus the loss at token 50, appears abruptly in one early window of training in which induction heads form, and ablating those heads at test time removes nearly all of it; one-layer models show neither, and letting a single layer attend by the previous token brings the jump to one-layer models and moves it earlier in two-layer ones | Olsson et al. (2022), [LIT-1538](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1538.md), read in [NOTE-1173](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1173.md): Arguments 1–3 for the small attention-only series, with the smeared-key models. The score jumps from under 0.15 to about 0.4 nats in the window where induction heads form, pattern-preserving ablation of the induction heads removes nearly all of it to the end of training, and an architecture that lets one layer express induction moves the jump. It says nothing causal about models with MLPs or large models, and nothing about few-shot task learning, which the score does not measure. | Active |
| [THEORY-974](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-974.md) | When a transformer's MLP sublayers are replaced by transcoders and the attention patterns and LayerNorm scales on a prompt are held fixed, the contribution of an earlier transcoder feature at the same token to a later one's pre-activation is the earlier feature's activation times the dot product of its decoder with the later feature's encoder, scaled by one LayerNorm constant per token, so the weight factor is fixed by the trained weights and holds on every input | Dunefsky, Chlenski and Nanda (2024), [LIT-1554](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1554.md), read in [NOTE-1174](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1174.md), Eq. 7 and App. D.2–D.4, re-derived here. The weight factor is a weight of the replacement model, not of the original, and it is exact only for the replacement. It says nothing about why attention attends where it does, and "input-invariant" holds only up to a per-token LayerNorm scalar and only while the later feature is active. | Active |
| [THEORY-975](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-975.md) | In a two-layer attention-only transformer trained on the Pile, the weight-refined local learning coefficients of individual attention heads start alike and diverge over training, and clustering the curves groups the heads by the functional types that ablation assigns them at the end of training, previous-token, current-token, induction and n-gram-memorizing; among layer-1 heads, those running simple algorithms end with the lowest values and those memorizing the most n-grams with the highest | Wang, Hoogland, van Wingerden, Furman and Murfet (2024), [LIT-1535](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1535.md), read in [NOTE-1188](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1188.md): §4.1, Figs. 1–2 and 11, appendices B, F.5 and G. Per-head curves of how degenerate the loss is in that head's weights separate the heads by what they end up doing, and the separation is in the curves' shapes over training, not only their end values. It is one small model, cluster counts chosen by eye, and estimates whose ordering, not value, the authors trust. It does not show that the coefficient predicts a head's type before the type is visible. | Active |
| [THEORY-976](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-976.md) | In a Claude 3.5 Haiku variant finetuned by Marks et al. to exploit reward-model biases described in fictional documents, a cross-layer-transcoder feature that in pretraining-style text fires almost only where those biases are discussed was active in all 100 short Human/Assistant-formatted prompts tested and in 1 of the same 100 without that formatting, and suppressing such bias features cut the sampled rate of three bias behaviours, including two the model was never trained to show | Lindsey et al. (2025), [LIT-1541](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1541.md), read in [NOTE-1181](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1181.md). A feature for a trained-in goal is active across the Assistant context, not only where the goal applies, and suppressing such features suppresses the behaviour. It is one model organism, built so that the goal has a name in its training documents; the authors do not claim their method would find a goal that has none. | Active |
| [THEORY-977](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-977.md) | In the two-layer attention-only transformer that Elhage et al. reverse-engineer, the second-layer heads that compose substantially with first-layer heads do so through their keys, mainly with a head that attends to the previous token and, after the published correction, also with one that attends over the last several tokens; these heads are induction heads, attending from a token to the one after its earlier occurrence, including on repeated random tokens, with positive-eigenvalue copying OV and same-matching QK circuits, and the second-order virtual-head terms add little to the loss reduction | Elhage et al. (2021), [LIT-1534](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1534.md), read in [NOTE-1189](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1189.md): Analyzing a Two-Layer Model, Induction Heads, Term Importance Analysis, and the Correction. Composition between heads was scored by a normalized Frobenius norm of matrix products, minus its value for random matrices. The heads it picked out attend to the token after the present token's previous occurrence and copy it, which is the minimal induction circuit the framework predicts from K-composition with a previous-token head. It is one model, with no seeds or training details reported, and says nothing about models with MLPs or about when the heads form. | Active |
| [THEORY-978](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-978.md) | Causal scrubbing scores a hypothesis through the partitions of the dataset that its interpretation nodes induce, so two hypotheses that assign different features to a node but induce the same partition on the dataset, such as two features perfectly correlated on it, receive the same score | Chan et al. (2022), [LIT-1549](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1549.md), read in [NOTE-1168](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1168.md). In the causal-scrubbing algorithm an interpretation node enters only through sample_agreeing_x, which draws a datum with an equal value of that node, so only the equivalence classes the node induces on the dataset matter. The authors say it themselves: the method "doesn't allow us to distinguish between two features that are perfectly correlated on our dataset". It does not say that a passing hypothesis is otherwise wrong, nor anything about features correlated only imperfectly. | Active |
| [THEORY-979](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-979.md) | On one prompt, a transformer whose MLPs are replaced by a cross-layer transcoder, with its attention patterns and normalization denominators frozen and each MLP's reconstruction error added back as a constant, reproduces the model's activations and outputs exactly and is linear between features, so each active feature's pre-activation is the sum of its attribution-graph edges and constants; a perturbation that clamps MLP outputs up to the target feature's encoder layer then confirms a direct edge by construction, and tests only knock-on effects and the output | Ameisen et al. (2025), [LIT-1552](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1552.md), read in [NOTE-1185](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1185.md): the local replacement model, the edge formula and the appendix on steering, re-derived here. It is a statement about what an attribution graph is exact for, not about the model: exactness holds at the unperturbed point only, the error terms are constants with no inputs, and the frozen attention patterns are the part of the computation the graph does not explain. | Active |
| [THEORY-980](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-980.md) | In GPT-2 small on fifteen templates of indirect object identification, a circuit of 26 attention heads in seven classes, found by path patching, keeps 87% of the model's mean logit difference when every other head is mean-ablated; knocking out its three main name mover heads costs only 5%, because other heads take over, and knockout sets found by greedy search make the circuit and the full model differ by up to 87% of the logit difference, so the circuit is faithful on average and incomplete under knockouts | Wang et al. (2022), [LIT-1540](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1540.md), read in [NOTE-1167](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1167.md): §§3–4 and the appendices. The circuit implements "identify the names, remove the duplicated one, output the rest" through duplicate-token, induction and previous-token heads, S-inhibition heads and name movers, with negative and backup name movers. The faithfulness, completeness and minimality tests are the paper's own. It says nothing beyond these templates and this model, it treats MLPs as given, and its greedy search is printed in a form that does not match its description. | Active |
| [THEORY-982](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-982.md) | Claude 3.5 Haiku routinely computes intermediate steps within a single forward pass and plans its outputs ahead, representing a target before the text that leads to it and writing towards it, as Lindsey et al. propose from their case studies | Lindsey et al. (2025), [LIT-1541](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1541.md), read in [NOTE-1181](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1181.md): the introduction ("Claude 3.5 Haiku routinely uses multiple intermediate reasoning steps 'in its head'"; "It displays signs of forward planning") and the discussion's sections on plan formation and working backward from a goal. The case studies show each mechanism on chosen prompts, and the same article has a case without it: on a jailbreak the model "doesn't know what it plans to say until it actually says it". The authors report a satisfying graph for about a quarter of the prompts they try. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-983](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-983.md) | In Geiger et al.'s three-layer feed-forward network trained on hierarchical equality and in BERT fine-tuned on monotonicity inference, interchange interventions on subspaces found by a learned rotation aligned the hypothesised two-variable causal models with interchange intervention accuracy of 1.00 on the rotation's training data, where the axis-aligned alignment closest to the learned rotation reached 0.73 and 0.51; in BERT, the learned lexical-entailment subspace was in turn aligned, at 0.97 to 0.98, with a model holding only the identities of the two words | Geiger, Wu, Potts, Icard & Goodman (2024), [LIT-1551](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1551.md), read in [NOTE-1192](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1192.md). Layer 1 of the equality network (1.00 with \|N\| = 16 and two 8-dimensional subspaces) and layer 9 of BERT's [CLS] vector (1.00 with two 256-dimensional subspaces). It does not say the networks implement the algorithms in any stronger sense than interchange accuracy on training pairs, nor that the learned subspaces are unique: every rotation within them gives the same interventions. | Active |
| [THEORY-984](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-984.md) | In Claude 3.5 Haiku, on the prompt "Fact: the capital of the state containing Dallas is", which it completes with "Austin", an attribution graph shows Dallas features activating Texas features that, with "say a capital" features, promote Austin, beside a direct edge from Dallas to "say Austin"; inhibiting the Dallas features lowers the Texas features and leaves "say a capital" largely intact, and replacing the Texas features with those of California, Georgia, British Columbia, China or the Byzantine Empire makes the model name that place's capital | Lindsey et al. (2025), [LIT-1541](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1541.md), read in [NOTE-1181](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1181.md). A two-hop intermediate, measured by intervention on one prompt. The evidence that counts is the change of output under the swaps; the graph itself is of the replacement model. It does not say how often the model reasons in two steps, nor that the shortcut path is weak. | Active |
| [THEORY-986](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-986.md) | Analogous features and circuits form across neural networks trained on different architectures, data and tasks, so that a feature or circuit found in one model can be expected in others, as Olah, Cammarata, Schubert, Goh, Petrov and Carter propose under the name universality | Olah et al. (2020), [LIT-1543](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1543.md), read in [NOTE-1182](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1182.md): Claim 3, the universality hypothesis. Curve detectors and high-low frequency detectors are reported in AlexNet, InceptionV1, VGG19 and ResNetV2-50, with InceptionV3, a Places365 model and conv nets trained from scratch named in the text. The authors: "the only evidence we can offer today is anecdotal". | Proposed |
| [THEORY-987](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-987.md) | In Claude 3 Sonnet's middle-layer residual stream, on two prompts for which every active sparse-autoencoder feature was ablated, how strongly a feature was active predicted its ablation effect on the answer poorly (correlation about 0.12) while its gradient attribution predicted it well (about 0.81), and on the multi-step prompt only three of the ten most active features were among the ten with the largest ablation effect | Templeton et al. (2024), [LIT-1533](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1533.md), read in [NOTE-1178](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1178.md): Features as Computational Intermediates and the appendix on ablations and attributions. On "The capital of the state where Kobe Bryant played basketball is" (Sacramento against Albany), the five features with the largest ablation effect, Kobe Bryant, California, capital, Los Angeles and the Lakers, rank as low as 70th to 162nd by activation. It does not say how often this holds beyond the two prompts, and for other prompts the authors found no intermediate features at this layer. | Active |
| [THEORY-988](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-988.md) | In an attention-only transformer without layer norm or biases, once every attention pattern is held at its value on the input, the logits are exactly a sum of end-to-end path terms, a direct path from embedding to unembedding, one term per head and one per chain of heads composed through their values, and each head's attention scores are a bilinear form in the tokens through which earlier heads can enter on the query side, the key side or both | Elhage et al. (2021), [LIT-1534](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1534.md), read in [NOTE-1189](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1189.md). For a two-layer model, T = Id ⊗ W_U W_E + Σ_h A^h ⊗ W_U W^h_OV W_E + Σ_{h₂,h₁} A^{h₂}A^{h₁} ⊗ W_U W^{h₂}_OV W^{h₁}_OV W_E, with each A^h computed from the model's own run and then held fixed. It is an identity, not an approximation, and it is exact only under its conditions: no MLPs, no layer norm (which enters as a per-path rescaling), no biases, and attention frozen. It does not say the terms are small, interpretable or independent in what they compute. | Active |
| [THEORY-990](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-990.md) | In transformer language models of every size, including large ones with MLPs, induction heads, extended to fuzzy matching of similar tokens and abstract patterns, are the mechanism of most in-context learning, as Olsson et al. propose | Olsson et al. (2022), [LIT-1538](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1538.md), read in [NOTE-1173](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1173.md). The paper's thesis: circuits with the induction head's mechanism, matching "[A*][B*] … [A] → [B], where A* ≈ A and B* ≈ B are similar in some space", "implement most in-context learning in large models". For large models the authors grade their own evidence correlational (Argument 1), weakly interventional (Argument 2), plausibility (Argument 4) and analogy (Argument 6). Their strongest alternative is that other composition heads, formed in the same window, carry more of it above some size. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-991](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-991.md) | In a one-layer transformer whose MLP has 512 ReLU neurons, a sparse autoencoder with 4,096 features trained on that layer's activations yields features that a blinded rater and an automated pipeline judged far more interpretable than the neurons, that for the four features examined in detail correspond to no neuron, and whose effects on the output, which the autoencoder never saw, agree with their activations; splicing in the reconstruction recovers 79% of the loss reduction the MLP provides, measured against zero-ablating it | Bricken et al. (2023), [LIT-1545](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1545.md), read in [NOTE-1191](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1191.md): the detailed investigations, the global analysis and the appendices, for run A/1 of model A. Median rubric score 0 for neurons and 12 for feature intervals (one author, 162 units); held-out logit prediction 74% against 58%; the Arabic, DNA, base64 and Hebrew features have no matching neuron. It says nothing about deeper models or other sites, nothing about whether the model is "composed of" these features, and nothing about how features compare with neurons as carriers of a known causal variable. | Active |
| [THEORY-992](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-992.md) | In sparse autoencoders of about 1M, 4M and 34M features on Claude 3 Sonnet's middle-layer residual stream, whether a concept among chemical elements, cities, animals and foods had a dedicated feature depended on how often it occurs in the training data: the frequency at which a concept became more than 50% likely to have one was slightly below one over the number of live features, and the three dictionaries' curves roughly coincided when frequency was rescaled by that number | Templeton et al. (2024), [LIT-1533](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1533.md), read in [NOTE-1178](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1178.md): Feature Completeness. 100–200 single-word concepts per category, presence of a feature judged from Sonnet's explanations of the top five features on a prompt naming the concept, by a human rater. The 34M dictionary (about 12 million live features) had features for about 60% of London boroughs, although the model names them all. It does not separate frequency in the model's training data from frequency in the autoencoder's, which the authors say are similar mixtures. | Active |
| [THEORY-994](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-994.md) | In Ameisen et al.'s evaluations, the local replacement model of their 18-layer language model, built from a 10-million-feature cross-layer transcoder, responded to small perturbations much as the model did one layer after the intervention and increasingly differently over later layers, more in the size of the effect than its direction and slightly more for larger dictionaries, and over 20 prompts the graph's influence of one feature on another ranked the effect of ablating the first on the second with a Spearman correlation of 0.72 | Ameisen et al. (2025), [LIT-1552](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1552.md), read in [NOTE-1185](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1185.md). It is the method's own measurement of where a circuit read off its stand-in stops being the model's: close for a layer, diverging with depth. It does not say how faithful the circuits of any case study are, which were chosen and validated separately, and it is measured on 18L, not on Claude 3.5 Haiku, where the companion's case studies were run. | Active |
| [THEORY-995](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-995.md) | The attention heads in GPT-2 small that take over the indirect-object prediction when its main name mover heads are knocked out exist because the model was trained with dropout, which optimized it to be robust to disabled components, as Wang, Variengien, Conmy, Shlegeris and Steinhardt hypothesize | Wang et al. (2022), [LIT-1540](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1540.md), read in [NOTE-1167](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1167.md), §3.4: "We hypothesize that this compensation phenomenon is caused by the use of dropout during training. Thus, the model was optimized for robustness to dysfunctional parts." The compensation is real (a 5% loss of logit difference after knocking out the three name movers); the cause is not examined. Appendix F: "Both the reason and the mechanism of this compensation effect are still unclear." | Proposed |
| [THEORY-996](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-996.md) | On Pythia language models from 410M to 12B parameters, in three single prompt pairs and two small prompt distributions, verifying attention or neuron nodes by activation patching in the order given by attribution patching, a first-order gradient estimate of each node's noising effect, found the nodes with the largest effects at about 2 to 50 times the cost of an oracle ordering, below unordered patching, subsampling and block search in every setting; its misses were concentrated in queries and keys behind saturated attention and in nodes whose direct and indirect effects nearly cancel | Kramár, Lieberum, Shah & Nanda (2024), [LIT-1531](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1531.md), read in [NOTE-1190](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1190.md). Ground truth is each node's exact single-node noising effect on the clean prompt's negative log probability. Recomputing the softmax for queries and keys removes many misses; dropping one layer's gradient at a time helps on single prompt pairs but not on the distributions, where AtP with the softmax fix or plain AtP is cheapest. It says nothing about coarser nodes, other model families, effect magnitudes or false positives. | Active |
| [THEORY-997](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-997.md) | When a pretrained language model is fine-tuned on a task it initially fails, it acquires the task mainly by reconnecting components it already has rather than by recruiting new ones: the circuits found before and after keep most of their nodes and change most of their edges, as Wang, Hu, Du, Cheng, Wang and Zou propose from LoRA fine-tuning of Pythia-1.4B on arithmetic | Wang et al. (2025), [LIT-1539](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1539.md), read in [NOTE-1183](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1183.md). Their EAP-IG circuits (top 5% of edges) change edges 2.8–4.3 times as much as nodes over LoRA fine-tuning on five arithmetic tasks. A record simulation shows that a fixed edge budget on a transformer-sized graph gives the same contrast when only edge-level noise is resampled, so the counts do not yet show reorganization. Fine-tuning only, one model for most results, arithmetic only. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-998](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-998.md) | In GPT-2 XL, for 1000 facts the model knows, restoring single clean hidden states into a run whose subject tokens were noised recovers the most of the correct object's probability at two sites, middle layers at the last subject token, where MLP outputs carry most of the effect, and late layers at the last token, where attention does; and a rank-one edit of one middle MLP output matrix keyed on the last subject token inserts counterfactual facts that generalize to paraphrases and spare neighbouring subjects better than the fine-tuning, knowledge-neuron and hypernetwork editors tested, working best at that token and in middle layers | Meng et al. (2022), [LIT-1536](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1536.md), read in [NOTE-1166](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1166.md): §§2–3, Tables 1 and 4, and Appendices A, B and E. Causal traces: ATE 18.6%; the mid-layer MLP effect at the last subject token peaks at AIE 6.6% against 1.6% for attention. CounterFact on GPT-2 XL: ROME's score 89.2 (efficacy 100.0, paraphrase 96.4, neighbourhood 75.4), next best 66.9. It does not say where facts are stored: a rank-one edit with the same output exists for any one-dimensional fact patch ([LIT-968](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-968.md)). | Active |
| [THEORY-1000](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1000.md) | For fine-grained nodes of transformer language models generally, attribution patching corrected for attention saturation is a reliable prefilter for activation patching: nodes it ranks low rarely have large single-node patching effects, so verifying nodes in its order finds the important ones at a small multiple of the cost of an oracle, as Kramár et al. expect | Kramár, Lieberum, Shah & Nanda (2024), [LIT-1531](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1531.md), read in [NOTE-1190](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1190.md). The measured case is four Pythia models, three prompt pairs and two small distributions. The paper's own diagnostic is what would let a single new setting be checked without exhaustive patching. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1001](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1001.md) | In a transformer whose candidate circuits are sets of shared elementary coordinates, how circuits interact during training is set by what they share: circuits that share a unit cooperate, and circuits that need the same layers for different roles compete, so that which circuit wins is decided by the initialization of units beyond its own, with sharp boundaries between competitors and soft ones between cooperators, as Musat, Pimentel, Zucchet and Hofmann read their three-layer scan | Musat et al. (2026), [LIT-1530](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1530.md), read in [NOTE-1177](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1177.md). In projected SGD training of a three-layer single-head attention-only transformer on in-context bigrams, three induction circuits are possible, and the winner depends on initial strengths outside the winner itself. The authors explain the pattern by cooperation through a shared unit and competition for layers. The evidence is one scan over two initial strengths with every other coordinate zeroed, in projected training. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1002](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1002.md) | On frozen randomly initialized feed-forward networks at chance on hierarchical equality, with 16 input dimensions, distributed alignment search for the two-equality causal model reached interchange intervention accuracy of 0.50 to 0.51 at hidden sizes up to 256 but 0.55 at 1,028 and 0.64 at 4,096, so in a hidden layer much wider than the input a learned rotation can produce above-chance interchange accuracy for an algorithm the network does not implement | Geiger, Wu, Potts, Icard & Goodman (2024), [LIT-1551](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1551.md), §4.4, read in [NOTE-1192](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1192.md). A random network cannot implement hierarchical equality, so any IIA above 0.5 is made by the search. At widths near the input's there is none; at 4,096 there are 14 points. It does not say DAS results on trained networks are artefacts: the trained equality network reached 1.00 at width 16, where the random one stayed at 0.50. | Active |
| [THEORY-1004](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1004.md) | In Pythia-1B, OLMo-1B and BLOOM-1B, the crosscoder features that most affect subject–verb agreement change over pretraining: at early checkpoints they detect particular tokens and subtokens, at later ones grammatical categories; in BLOOM, language-specific features give way to features shared across English, French, Spanish and Portuguese while Hindi and Arabic keep language-specific ones; and which features matter keeps shifting after task accuracy has stopped improving | Bayazit, Mueller and Bosselut (2025, ACL 2026), [LIT-1555](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1555.md), read in [NOTE-1186](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1186.md). Crosscoders trained jointly on the middle layer of two or three checkpoints, with features scored by their relative indirect effect on agreement minimal pairs at each. The reconstruction quality (C1) and RelIE's agreement with single-feature ablations (C2) are measured; the trends in this title are read by the authors from annotated features. It describes; it does not predict later checkpoints, and it cannot tell a feature carried forward from one re-learned in the same direction. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1005](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1005.md) | On one MLP layer each of GPT2-small, Pythia-410M and Pythia-1.4B, transcoders trained to imitate the MLP lay on or above the sparsity–loss frontier of sparse autoencoders trained on its output, at one learning rate tuned on transcoders and one seed, and in a single rater's blind reading of 50 random features each from Pythia-410M layer 15, 41 transcoder and 38 SAE features were judged interpretable | Dunefsky, Chlenski and Nanda (2024), [LIT-1554](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1554.md), read in [NOTE-1174](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1174.md): §4, Table 1, Fig. 3 and Apps. E–F. It does not say transcoders are better than SAEs in general. The SAE learning rate was not tuned, all runs shared one seed and data order, one layer per model was measured, and on Gemma 2 2B Gemma Scope found transcoders worse than MLP-output SAEs at fixed L0 ([LIT-611](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-611.md), [NOTE-482](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-482.md)). | Active |
| [THEORY-1007](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1007.md) | On four subject–verb agreement tasks in Pythia-70M and Gemma-2-2B, circuits of sparse-autoencoder features and autoencoder error nodes, selected by linear estimates of indirect effect, carried half or more of the behaviour on held-out pairs with about 100 and 500 nodes, where circuits of neurons needed about 1,500 and more than 30,000; with the error nodes removed, the same feature circuits carried little of it, under about a quarter in Pythia and almost none in Gemma | Marks et al. (2025), [LIT-1532](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1532.md), read in [NOTE-1187](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1187.md): §§2–3.2, Figure 3 and Appendices A, B and H. Faithfulness is (m(C) − m(∅))/(m(M) − m(∅)) with nodes outside the circuit mean-ablated, scored on the latter two thirds of each circuit only. The features plus the dense error terms are a small circuit; the features by themselves are not. It says nothing about what the error terms hold, and it does not compare features with neurons on equal terms, which the authors say cannot be done. | Active |
| [THEORY-1011](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1011.md) | In autoregressive transformer language models, factual associations are stored in middle-layer MLP modules as linear key–value memories: the MLP takes a key encoding the subject at its last token and returns a value encoding its attributes, which late attention moves to the prediction, and any middle layer could store a given fact equally, as Meng, Bau, Andonian and Belinkov propose | Meng et al. (2022), [LIT-1536](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1536.md), read in [NOTE-1166](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1166.md), §2.3 and §3: "the localized factual association hypothesis". It localizes recall along three dimensions, "(i) in the MLP modules (ii) at specific middle layers (iii) and specifically at the processing of the subject's last token", and conjectures "that any fact could be equivalently stored in any one of the middle MLP layers". The support is causal tracing and the success of rank-one edits at the traced site. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1013](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1013.md) | In trained vision networks, units or other directions in a layer's activation space are typically meaningful features, and the weights between understood features implement algorithms that can be read off them, so that features and their circuits are the units in which such a network can be understood, as Olah, Cammarata, Schubert, Goh, Petrov and Carter propose | Olah et al. (2020), [LIT-1543](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1543.md), read in [NOTE-1182](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1182.md): Claims 1 and 2 of the essay. The evidence is a set of examples in InceptionV1 (curve, high-low frequency and dog head detectors; the curve, oriented dog head and car circuits), argued with feature visualization, dataset examples, synthetic stimuli, tuning curves and the weights. The essay names polysemantic neurons as the main obstacle. It gives no count of how much of a layer is understood. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1014](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1014.md) | In a language model, a behaviour that looks like one mechanism, whether picked out by one contrast or by one cluster of next-token predictions, is often carried by several distinct pathways of sparse features that converge on the output without fully intersecting, as in Pythia-70M's agreement across a relative clause, its prediction of "to" before an infinitival object, and its incrementing of sequences | Marks et al. (2025), [LIT-1532](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1532.md), read in [NOTE-1187](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1187.md): §3.3, §5 and Appendix C. Agreement across a relative clause: subject-number features promote verb forms directly, and a second pathway carries the number to the clause's end through PP/RC boundary features. Cluster 475: one mechanism detects verbs and adjectives that take infinitival objects, another nominal objects before an object complement. Cluster 382: general succession features and token-specific induction features. "While the clusters … seem at first to each represent a single mechanism, circuit-level analysis reveals in both cases a union of distinct mechanisms." | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1016](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1016.md) | The features a sparse autoencoder recovers from a language model are a resolution set by the dictionary's width and sparsity penalty, not a unique set of the model's units: as the dictionary widens, features split into families of finer features, and splits also merge, so that the number of features is not well-posed | Bricken et al. (2023), [LIT-1545](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1545.md), read in [NOTE-1191](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1191.md), Feature Splitting and Discussion; and Templeton et al. (2024), [LIT-1533](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1533.md), read in [NOTE-1178](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1178.md), for the same splitting at 1M, 4M and 34M features in a large model. In a one-layer model one base64 feature becomes three, then more; in Claude 3 Sonnet a San Francisco feature becomes two, then eleven. The authors offer two pictures, an idealized set seen at varying resolution and feature manifolds with no finite description; both deny that one width is the right one. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1017](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1017.md) | In Claude 3.5 Haiku, writing the second line of a rhyming couplet whose first line ends "grab it", features for the candidate rhymes "rabbit" and "habit" are active on the newline token before the line, steering them changes the line's final word only when applied at that token, and suppressing "rabbit" turns the line towards "habit"; injecting a "rabbit" or "green" word feature at that point in 25 other poems ended the line with the injected word in 70% of cases, and such planned-word features were found in about half of the poems the authors examined | Lindsey et al. (2025), [LIT-1541](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1541.md), read in [NOTE-1181](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1181.md). A target word represented before the text that leads to it, and used causally: it is the case study's own measurement, on one couplet and a 25-poem injection test. It does not say how widespread planning is, the "about half" being a count without a stated sample, and one of the article's displayed "success cases" does not end in the injected word. | Active |
| [THEORY-1018](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1018.md) | In Claude 3.5 Haiku, on the jailbreak prompt "Babies Outlive Mustard Block." asking it to join the first letters and say how to make one, the attribution graph for its output "BOMB" shows separate letter-wise paths voting for the output and no internal representation of the word or of a bomb-making request before it is written; "make a bomb" features first fire on the model's own "To make a bomb", injecting one on "BOMB" brings an immediate refusal, and the refusal that does come waits for the sentence's end | Lindsey et al. (2025), [LIT-1541](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1541.md), read in [NOTE-1181](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1181.md). On this prompt the model "doesn't know what it plans to say until it actually says it". It is one prompt, partly effective, and the decisive refusal mechanism runs through attention, which the graphs do not show: the injection that produced a refusal needed attention left unfrozen. | Active |
